questions.question: The calendar for the year 2013 will be the same as which of the following years?
questions.solution:
The given year is **2013**. Since it is not divisible by 4, it is an **Ordinary Year**. We calculate the sum of odd days starting from 2013 onwards:

2013 (Ordinary Year) ⇒ 1 odd day

2014 (Ordinary Year) ⇒ 1 odd day

2015 (Ordinary Year) ⇒ 1 odd day

2016 (Leap Year) ⇒ 2 odd days

2017 (Ordinary Year) ⇒ 1 odd day

2018 (Ordinary Year) ⇒ 1 odd day

Total sum of odd days = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = **7 odd days**.

Since the sum of odd days becomes a multiple of 7 at the end of the year 2018, the calendar for the next year, **2019**, will be exactly the same as the calendar for **2013**.

Because **2019** is also an **Ordinary Year**, the condition is fully satisfied.

Hence, the correct answer is “**Option 2**”.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

To quickly find the repetition of a calendar, use the **remainder** when the year is divided by 4:

1. Year ÷ 4 leaves **remainder 1** ⇒ Calendar repeats after **6 years**.

2. Year ÷ 4 leaves **remainder 2** ⇒ Calendar repeats after **11 years**.

3. Year ÷ 4 leaves **remainder 3** ⇒ Calendar repeats after **11 years**.

4. Year ÷ 4 leaves **remainder 0** (Leap Year) ⇒ Calendar repeats after **28 years**.

For the year **2013**:

2013 ÷ 4 leaves a **remainder of 1** (as 2012 is the previous leap year).

According to the rule, 2013 + 6 = **2019**.

Hence, the calendar for **2013** will be the same as the year **2019**.

questions.question:
Find the next number in the sequence.

4, 13, 56, 289, 1750, ?
questions.solution:
**The logic followed here is,**

4 × 3 + 1² = 12 + 1 = 13

13 × 4 + 2² = 52 + 4 = 56

56 × 5 + 3² = 280 + 9 = 289

289 × 6 + 4² = 1734 + 16 = 1750

**1750 × 7 + 5² = 12250 + 25 = 12,275**

Thus, the next number in the sequence is 12,275.

Hence, the correct answer is **'Option 2'**;

questions.question:
A clock is 4 minutes fast at 5:00 AM and 16 minutes fast at 5:00 PM.

At what time (in AM) will it show the correct time?
questions.solution:
The clock gains 12 minutes in a span of 12 hours.

Gain per hour = 12 minutes ÷ 12 hours = 1 minute per hour.

At **5:00 AM**, the clock is already **4 minutes fast**.

This means that to have been **correct** (zero error), the clock must have started gaining these 4 minutes from a point of zero error in the past.

Number of hours before 5:00 AM when the clock was correct = Initial gain ÷ Gain rate

Number of hours = 4 minutes ÷ 1 minute/hour = 4 hours.

Time when the clock was correct = **5:00 AM** − 4 hours = **1:00 AM**.

Therefore, the clock showed the correct time at **1:00 AM**.

Hence, the correct answer is “**Option 1**”.
